subtype: Faces shaped for peers and cameras [Regulating]
passage: Chaitanya, you asked why I always do the same face in photos. Fine, since you're my oldest friend, this is Binita's confession. In Class 8, everyone in our group started doing this half-pout, chin down, one eyebrow up. I practised it in the bathroom mirror for a week. Now it just happens the second a phone comes out. Last month at Riya's birthday I did the pout in every single picture, and everyone commented that I looked so chill. Honestly? I'd had a fight at home that morning and wanted to leave the whole evening. The face was fine. I wasn't. Sometimes I scroll back and I can't tell which photos I was actually happy in. The only one I'm sure about is that blurry one you took, where I'm laughing with rice in my mouth.

qa.q: Where did Binita practise the photo face?
qa.a: In the bathroom mirror, for a week.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling at Riya's birthday behind the pout?
qa.a: Binita felt upset after a fight at home that morning and wanted to leave all evening, even though the photos looked chill.

qa.q: What could Binita try if the practised face starts to feel like a mask?
qa.a: Keep some unposed photos and tell a close friend like Chaitanya how the day really went, instead of letting the face do all the talking.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the blurry photo?
qa.a: Chaitanya may see it as the truest picture of Binita, catching real laughter instead of the practised face.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager's practised photo face signalling belonging while the private mood underneath is different.

subtype: Snarl or scowl as a warning sign [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Neel, and I was two seats away in the computer lab when it started. Vishal had lost his saved project and was sure Tanuja had logged him out. He turned, and his whole face changed: lip curled, eyes narrowed, jaw pushed forward. He stood up and took a step towards her desk. Tanuja didn't argue back. She rolled her chair away, put the desk between them and said, quite evenly, "I didn't touch your login. Let's ask Sir." Vishal slammed his palm on the monitor. That's when Tanuja walked straight to Mr Joshi at the front, and he came over at once, calmed Vishal down and recovered the file from the backup. Later Tanuja told me her hands had been shaking the whole time. I wouldn't have known. She looked so calm.

qa.q: What had Vishal lost?
qa.a: His saved project.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling as she rolled her chair away?
qa.a: Tanuja was frightened, as her shaking hands showed, but kept calm on the outside and read Vishal's face as a warning.

qa.q: Which of Tanuja's steps kept things safe?
qa.a: She moved back and put the desk between them, spoke evenly without arguing, and went straight to Mr Joshi once Vishal slammed the monitor.

qa.q: What might Vishal have been feeling when his face changed?
qa.a: Vishal was probably angry and panicked about losing the project, and blamed Tanuja before checking.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a peer's snarl as possible threat, stepping back, staying calm and involving an adult when it escalates, as seen by a classmate.

passage: Omkar, you think the new boy is smirking at you? First hear your Bhupen Mama's story. At fifteen, in our school in Guwahati, a boy called Pabitra joined my class. Every time I answered in English, one corner of his mouth went up. Just one. I was sure he was laughing at my accent. For a month I avoided him and even told friends he was proud. Then in the football final we were on the same team, and after I scored, he ran up with that same lopsided smile, hugged me and said, very quietly, "Well done." That was his whole smile, Omkar. Half a smile was all his shy face ever managed. We stayed friends for forty years. So before you decide about this boy, watch him somewhere else. Ask him something.

qa.q: When did Bhupen realise the lopsided smile wasn't mocking?
qa.a: In the football final, when Pabitra ran up with the same smile after Bhupen scored, hugged him and said "Well done."

qa.q: What did young Bhupen feel when Pabitra smiled on one side?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and resentful, sure that Pabitra was laughing at his accent.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Bhupen's reading of the smile?
qa.a: Seeing the same half smile in a warm moment on the football team showed it was habit and shyness, not mockery.

qa.q: How might Pabitra have experienced that first month?
qa.a: Pabitra, shy and new, may have felt lonely and confused about why Bhupen kept avoiding him.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reading a one-sided smile as mockery when it was habit and shyness, and context changing its meaning.

passage:
Thursday, late
Smiled all day again. Smiled at the bus stop, smiled in chemistry, smiled when Ritika showed me her new bag. It's easier than people asking what's wrong, because I don't even know what's wrong, only that everything has felt grey since Nani passed in March.
Then in the library, Pradeep Sir handed back my essay and said, "Good work. You look tired these days, though. The smile's there, but the rest of you isn't." I laughed it off. He didn't push. He just said, "My room's open at lunch on Tuesdays and Fridays, if you ever want somewhere quiet. Talk or don't talk."
I nearly cried in the corridor. When I got home I told Mumma about the grey feeling. She held my hand for a long time and said we'd go and see the school counsellor together.
Himani

qa.q: When did Nani pass away?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: Why did Himani keep smiling all day?
qa.a: Himani felt low and grey but kept smiling to avoid questions, partly because the sadness was hard to explain even to Himani.

qa.q: What made Pradeep Sir's approach work?
qa.a: He named what he saw kindly, didn't press, and offered a clear, low-pressure time to come, whether to talk or just sit.

qa.q: What might Pradeep Sir have noticed?
qa.a: He noticed the smile didn't match the tiredness in the rest of Himani's face, and chose a gentle offer instead of questions.

grounding: It shows a teenager masking low mood with a smile and a trusted adult noticing that it doesn't reach the rest of the face, offering an open door without pressure.

subtype: Controlling a frown at a parent or teacher [Regulating]
passage: I'm Ganga, Sahil's cousin, and I was at their dinner table when Chacha said the Goa trip with Sahil's friends was off because exams were close. Sahil said, "Okay, Papa." He was smiling slightly, but I could see a small muscle jumping in his forehead, and his eyebrows kept pulling together and then smoothing out, as if he were ironing them flat. Chacha didn't notice; he was busy with the rasam. After dinner Sahil sat on the balcony for a long time. Then he went back in and said, "Papa, I said okay, but I don't agree. I've finished revising three subjects. Can we talk about it?" Chacha looked surprised, then pulled out a chair. I don't know how it ended, but they talked for an hour.

qa.q: How many subjects had Sahil finished revising?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What might the muscle jumping in Sahil's forehead suggest?
qa.a: Sahil was probably frustrated and disappointed about the cancelled trip, trying to hide it behind a slight smile and 'Okay, Papa'.

qa.q: Why was Sahil's second approach clearer than his face?
qa.a: Saying 'I don't agree' and giving his reason put the disagreement into words Chacha couldn't miss, which opened a real talk.

qa.q: How might Chacha have read Sahil's first "Okay, Papa"?
qa.a: Busy with the rasam, Chacha likely took it as easy agreement, missing the tense forehead Ganga saw.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager smoothing a frown to avoid conflict with a parent while the forehead stays tense, then putting the disagreement into words, seen by a cousin.

subtype: Eyebrows in teasing and flirt-free banter [Expressing]
passage:
Monday: "I'm going to top the physics test," Mehak announced. Pallavi raised one eyebrow slowly, as high as it would go. Mehak burst out laughing and shoved her. "Okay, okay. But watch me."
Wednesday: Joanna, who had joined in August, said in the canteen that she'd been to three concerts this year. Pallavi's eyebrow shot up the same way. Joanna's smile faded; she went quiet and left half her sandwich. Mehak nudged Pallavi under the table.
Friday: Pallavi caught Joanna at the lockers. "About Wednesday, the eyebrow. With Mehak it's our joke. I think with you it looked like I didn't believe you. Sorry." Joanna let out a long breath. "I did think that." "Tell me about the concerts properly?" Pallavi asked, and this time she just listened.

qa.q: How many concerts did Joanna say she had been to this year?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What was Joanna feeling when her smile faded?
qa.a: Joanna felt hurt and embarrassed, unsure whether the raised eyebrow meant disbelief or a joke.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do to repair things?
qa.a: She named the eyebrow, explained it was an in-joke with Mehak, apologised, and then listened properly 🙂

qa.q: How did Mehak take the same eyebrow on Monday?
qa.a: Mehak knew it as their shared joke, a playful challenge, so it made her laugh rather than sting.

grounding: It shows a raised eyebrow reading as playful banter between close friends but stinging a newer classmate who is unsure it is a joke.

passage:
Sangeeta: u ok?? Ma'am looked SO annoyed in 3rd period 😬
Urmila: she thought I was bored. my eyes kept closing
Sangeeta: were u bored tho
Urmila: no!! I love bio. I was up till 2 finishing the video edit for the fest
Sangeeta: 2?? 😴
Urmila: Ma'am kept me back after class. I thought she'd shout
Sangeeta: did she
Urmila: no. she asked how I'd been sleeping. I told her about the edit and the phone in bed
Sangeeta: and??
Urmila: she said heavy eyes aren't rude but let's fix the reason. told me to share the edit with the fest team and charge my phone outside my room tonight
Sangeeta: wow she's nice
Urmila: yeah. felt bad she thought I didn't care about her class

qa.q: Until what time was Urmila up the night before?
qa.a: Until 2, finishing the video edit for the fest.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when Ma'am kept Urmila back after class?
qa.a: Urmila was anxious, expecting to be shouted at, and later felt bad that Ma'am had thought Urmila didn't care about biology.

qa.q: What did Ma'am do well?
qa.a: She asked about sleep before assuming disrespect, then suggested practical fixes: sharing the edit and charging the phone outside the room.

qa.q: How did Ma'am first read Urmila's closing eyes?
qa.a: At first she looked annoyed, reading them as boredom, but she checked about sleep before deciding.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager's heavy, half-closed eyes after late screen time looking like boredom, and a teacher asking about sleep before assuming rudeness.

subtype: Winking and eyelid flutter in social play [Mismatch]
passage:
Lab supervisor's note, Wednesday
During the titration practical, Sumit winked at Omkar across the bench when Omkar's flask turned bright pink too early. Omkar winked back and both grinned; it was clearly their private joke about Omkar always overshooting. A few minutes later, Sumit winked at Prachi when she asked to borrow his clamp. Prachi's face tightened; she took the clamp without a word and moved to the far bench. I don't think Sumit meant anything by it, but Prachi had no way of knowing that. After class I spoke to Sumit on his own. He looked surprised and said it was "just a thanks". I explained that a wink only works when the other person is in on the joke. He agreed to talk to Prachi, and before the end of the day I checked with her: he had apologised, and she said she was fine.

qa.q: What happened to Omkar's flask during the titration?
qa.a: It turned bright pink too early.

qa.q: What did Prachi's tightened face suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Prachi likely felt uncomfortable and uneasy, perhaps reading the wink as flirting or mockery, since she wasn't in on any joke.

qa.q: What steps did the supervisor take, and why did they help?
qa.a: Speaking to Sumit privately, explaining when a wink works, and checking with Prachi the same day, so her discomfort was taken seriously.

qa.q: Why might Sumit have been surprised by Prachi's reaction?
qa.a: To Sumit it was 'just a thanks', like the friendly wink with Omkar, so he didn't expect it to land differently with Prachi.

grounding: It shows a wink working as a shared joke between friends but being misread by someone outside the joke, noted by a supervising adult.

subtype: Averting gaze as avoidance or respect [Interpreting]
passage:
Dear Ritu Didi,
You told me to write when something at the new school confused me, so here it is. My lab partner, Hafsa, never looks at me. In the first week I was sure she disliked me or thought I was stupid. Then I remembered what you said about Nani never looking straight at elders' faces, out of respect. It could be shyness too. Or maybe guilt about something? I didn't want to guess forever, so yesterday I asked, as gently as I could, "Is it okay if I look at the worksheet instead of at you? I don't know what's comfortable for you." Hafsa actually smiled at the worksheet. She said she's autistic and eye contact feels too loud for her; she listens better looking at the table. We finished the whole practical, and she laughed at my joke about the Bunsen burner.
Write back soon,
Usha

qa.q: What does Hafsa say eye contact feels like?
qa.a: Too loud for her.

qa.q: What did Usha feel in the first week?
qa.a: Usha felt hurt and unsure, convinced that Hafsa disliked Usha or thought Usha was stupid.

qa.q: Why was Usha's gentle question better than guessing?
qa.a: Usha listed several possible reasons but checked kindly instead of choosing one, which avoided treating Hafsa as rude and made the partnership work.

qa.q: What might it be like for Hafsa when Usha offers to look at the worksheet?
qa.a: Hafsa likely felt relieved and understood, free to listen in the way that suits her; she smiled and later laughed at Usha's joke 🤍

grounding: It illustrates a teenager weighing several readings of a peer's averted gaze, including respect, shyness and comfort, and asking gently instead of assuming.

passage:
"Rekha, don't turn round. That man by the paan shop is staring again."
"The one in the grey cap? He was there yesterday too."
"Every day this week. He doesn't look away even when I look at him. My stomach goes funny."
"Then your stomach's right. Come on, let's stand with the aunties near the sweet shop."
"Maybe I'm overreacting. He hasn't said anything."
"He doesn't need to say anything. Staring like that isn't your fault. We're telling someone today."
They walked back to the school gate, where Mrs Thomas, the vice principal, was seeing off the buses. Sonali told her everything. Mrs Thomas listened, said, "You were right to trust that feeling," and asked the guard to walk the girls to the stop. Then she phoned Sonali's father and the local beat constable before the bus had even come.

qa.q: What was the staring man wearing?
qa.a: A grey cap.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she said her stomach goes funny?
qa.a: Sonali felt uneasy and frightened, yet also unsure, wondering if it was an overreaction.

qa.q: What did Mrs Thomas do that made Sonali safer?
qa.a: She listened, backed Sonali's feeling, had the guard walk them to the stop, and phoned Sonali's father and the beat constable straight away.

qa.q: How did Rekha see Sonali's worry?
qa.a: Rekha took it seriously: the uneasy feeling was right, the staring wasn't Sonali's fault, and they had to tell someone that day.

grounding: It shows a teenager trusting discomfort at a persistent stare, moving towards other people and telling a trusted adult who acts the same day.
